paragraphs.heading: The ability to choose
paragraphs.edited: The ability to choose. In fact, so many questions about why things happen are answered simply by humanity's ability to make a choice. Choices really are what govern so much of our lives, from the easiest decisions to some of the hardest, from choices that take forever to make to ones we make in an instant. Choices are so powerful. They are a privilege and they are a responsibility, and they are something that God has given us. This is one of those pointers, again, to who God is and to the fact that he exists.

paragraphs.heading: Two things to nail down
paragraphs.edited: So we are challenging students with two things. Number one, that our free will points us to him. The fact that we have free will is a pointer to who he is. It helps us understand that because we have the ability to choose, God is out there somewhere. But number two, our free will should reflect him, and how we behave as Christians ought to be a reflection of who he is.

paragraphs.heading: Take your community's temperature
paragraphs.edited: So as you go about your unit this week, I want you to keep something in mind. Last week we took the temperature of our students to figure out where the students are. This week I want you to take the temperature of your community. We talked at the very beginning about the importance of establishing a community — a strong community, a community that is open, one that loves, one that's close, one that students feel safe in. We talked about that as kind of an overarching goal: that being able to communicate truth and love means having a community where students feel safe to ask questions and so forth.

paragraphs.heading: Four questions for leaders
paragraphs.edited: So here are a couple of things I want you to think about. Are leaders providing the right atmosphere? Are they crafting that sort of atmosphere of discussion — one where questions are welcome, one of grace and love but with truth, not letting one student dominate, inviting all students to participate? All of those pieces of the puzzle: is the right kind of atmosphere being fostered?

paragraphs.edited: Number two, are students being loved? And are they being challenged? So often we kind of confuse the two, and we think that we are loving students when really we are just letting them think what they want to think. In my experience, the most challenged students that I had — in terms of how much I challenged them — were the ones who felt most loved at the end of a year. Those are the ones who felt like they were valued.

If you notice, go back to those schools and ask those teachers how many graduates come back to see them. The number is probably pretty high. It sort of works this way: the more challenging you are with a student, the greater the respect you gain and the greater the love that you are showing them. It just works that way. So make sure that you love them, but make sure that you also challenge them.

paragraphs.heading: Almost at the halfway point
paragraphs.edited: All right, so you've almost made it to the halfway point. Congratulations, keep it up. You guys are doing a great job, I am sure. And remember, some of your students might be starting to feel some of the stress of school, because you're probably getting around midterms and finals and tests and quizzes and those kinds of things. So now would be a really good time, and this is a really good lesson, to do some fun things, to have some fun with students on making choices — whether it be through games, whether it be through examples, something silly, where you could have a whole bunch of fun having students make choices but at the same time teach them the power of those choices.
